passages.t: Ask God's word, and promise to obey it
passages.happening:
All the commanders, with Johanan son of Kareah and Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least to the greatest, come to Jeremiah (verse 1). They ask him to pray to the LORD his God for this remnant, so few out of so many (verse 2), that God will show them the way to walk and the thing to do (verse 3). Jeremiah agrees to pray and to tell them everything God answers, holding nothing back (verse 4).

They swear: may the LORD be a true and faithful witness against them if they do not act on every word God sends (verse 5). ‘Whether it is pleasant or unpleasant, we will obey the voice of the LORD our God to whom we are sending you’ (verse 6).

After ten days the word comes (verse 7). Jeremiah calls them all together (verse 8). God says that if they stay in the land, ‘then I will build you up and not tear you down; I will plant you and not uproot you’ (verse 10), for he grieves over the disaster he has brought. ‘Do not be afraid of the king of Babylon, whom you now fear’ (verse 11). God is with them to save them, and he will show them compassion, so that the king of Babylon will have compassion on them and let them stay in their land (verses 11 and 12).
passages.hearers:
The survivors had good reason to be afraid. Babylon had appointed Gedaliah, and his murder, with the killing of Babylonian soldiers, would look like rebellion. Babylon had already shown what it did to rebels. Egypt was the traditional refuge for people fleeing trouble in Canaan.

Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah appears in the next chapter as Azariah son of Hoshaiah. He may be one man with two names, or one name may have changed in copying.

The ten days of waiting matter. Jeremiah did not answer from his own judgment. He waited until God spoke.

God's answer repeats the words of Jeremiah's call: build and plant, not tear down and uproot. After the disaster, God says he grieves over it. The same God who judged now offers to stay with them and save them, in the very land they want to leave.
passages.later: The law had warned Israel's kings never to send the people ‘back to Egypt’ (Deuteronomy 17:16). Isaiah had said, ‘Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help’ (Isaiah 31:1).
passages.asks: The people promised to obey God whether the answer was pleasant or not. Ask whether you have ever asked God for guidance after you had already decided. And ask what it would look like to wait ten days for an answer rather than act on fear.

passages.happening:
But if they say they will not stay, and so disobey the LORD (verse 13), if they say they will go to Egypt, where they will see no war, hear no trumpet and not go hungry (verse 14), then they must hear the LORD's word (verse 15). The sword they fear will overtake them in Egypt, and the famine they dread will follow them there, and they will die there (verse 16). All who set their faces to go to Egypt will die by sword, famine and plague, with no survivor (verse 17). As God's anger was poured out on Jerusalem, so it will be poured out on them in Egypt (verse 18).

The LORD has told them not to go to Egypt (verse 19). They have deceived themselves, Jeremiah says, by sending him to God and promising to do whatever God said (verse 20). He has told them today, and they have not obeyed (verse 21). So they will die in the place where they want to go to live (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Egypt promised everything the survivors wanted: no war, no alarm, no hunger. From a purely practical point of view, going looked wise.

The text does not say Egypt was evil in itself. Abraham and Jacob's family had gone there in famine. The trouble was that God had given a specific word for this moment, and the people had asked for it and sworn to obey it.

Egypt was also the house of slavery from which God had first rescued Israel. To flee back there was to undo the exodus.

Jeremiah sees in their faces, before they answer, that they will not obey. Verses 19 to 22 are said as if their refusal has already happened, and the next chapter shows that it had.
passages.later: Hosea had asked the same of the north: ‘Will they not return to the land of Egypt and be ruled by Assyria because they refused to repent?’ (Hosea 11:5). Kings records that ‘all the people’ fled to Egypt ‘for fear of the Chaldeans’ (2 Kings 25:26).
passages.hard:
Why was going to Egypt wrong? Wasn't it sensible to flee from a dangerous empire?

From a purely strategic point of view, fleeing looked prudent, and the fear was reasonable after the killing of Babylonian soldiers. The text does not claim Egypt was evil in itself; Abraham and Jacob's family went there in famine. The issue is that God had spoken a specific word for this moment, and the people had asked for it and sworn to obey it. Going was disobedience to a direct command, not simply a bad tactical choice. There is also the background of Egypt as the house of slavery, and Deuteronomy 17:16 warned against returning.

The chapter teaches that real safety is found in obedience, and that no place is safe from the results of refusing God. It is not a rule against seeking refuge from danger, and these notes draw no line from it to any nation or to refugees today.
passages.asks: The people promised to obey and then refused when the answer was not what they wanted. Ask whether there is something God has told you that you are hoping he will change. And ask where you have gone looking for a place with no war and no hunger, instead of staying where God asked.
